claim: Chinese "magic mirrors" — 透光鏡, literally light-penetration mirrors — do what they are said to do. The face is polished bronze and reflects normally; the back carries a cast relief design. Shine a bright light on the polished face and reflect it onto a wall, and the pattern from the back appears in the projected disc, as though the solid metal were transparent. Examples survive from at least the 5th century, with claims of Han-dynasty manufacture, and only a handful are held in Western collections — one was identified in storage at the Cincinnati Art Museum in 2022. The effect is a manufacturing artifact, not an optical mystery: the mirror is cast flat with the design on the back, then the face is scraped and polished into a slight convexity. Where the casting is thinner — behind the relief — the metal flexes away under the scraping tool and takes less pressure than the thicker regions. When the tool is removed those thin areas rebound into marginally greater convexity, leaving a relief map of the back on the front in surface curvature far too slight to see directly, but enough to modulate a reflected beam. The pattern is on the front the whole time.

sources.label: Chinese magic mirror — overview of the type, the surviving examples and the differential-polishing explanation.

notes: Backstage. The phenomenon is not in dispute and the mechanism is textbook, but both sources here are secondary. The primary chain runs through Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 4 pt. 1 (which reproduces Shen Kuo's 11th-century Dream Pool Essays discussion, the earliest known attempt at an explanation) and the 1960s Berry/Mukai optical analyses.
